MET: Sells group life, dental and disability insurance to employers, plus retirement and annuity products; earnings depend on the investment yield on a very large fixed income portfolio.
B: Mines gold and copper across Africa, the Americas and Papua New Guinea, holding tier-one deposits alongside the jurisdictional risk that comes with several of them.
FIX: Installs and services the mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems inside commercial buildings, with data centres now the fastest-growing end market in its backlog.
D: Regulated electric utility serving Virginia, where the density of data centres in Loudoun County has made load growth the central planning problem.
BE: Sells solid-oxide fuel cells that generate power on site from natural gas or hydrogen, sold to data centres and industrial customers waiting for a grid connection.
COR: Distributes prescription drugs from manufacturers to pharmacies and hospitals at very thin margins on very large volume, plus specialty and oncology services.
BKR: Sells oilfield equipment and services, and separately the gas turbines and compressors that LNG plants are built around — the second half is the growth.
O: REIT owning freestanding retail properties let to a single tenant on long triple-net leases, paying its dividend monthly, which is most of its retail following.
TEL: Makes connectors and sensors for cars, aircraft, factories and data centres; the content per electric vehicle is materially higher than per combustion one.
NUE: Melts scrap in electric arc furnaces to make steel, a lower-cost and less capital-intensive process than a blast furnace, and sells joists, decking and rebar downstream.
TRGP: Gathers, processes and transports natural gas liquids from the Permian to the Gulf Coast for export; fee-based on volume with some commodity exposure.
SRE: Utility holding company owning San Diego Gas & Electric, the Texas transmission utility Oncor, and LNG export terminals on the Gulf Coast.
NXPI: Makes chips for cars — radar, in-vehicle networking, battery management — and for secure identification and payment; automotive is over half of revenue.
DAL: Runs the US airline with the strongest premium cabin and loyalty economics, where the American Express co-brand contributes a large and steadier share of profit than seats do.
F: Builds and sells trucks and SUVs, with the F-Series the profit centre, plus Ford Credit and a loss-making electric vehicle unit being retrenched.
OKE: Owns natural gas gathering, processing and NGL pipelines from the Bakken and Permian to the Gulf, earning fees on volume rather than on price.
FANG: Permian shale producer with the lowest cost structure among the pure plays, having consolidated acreage rather than expanded into other basins.
PSA: REIT owning self-storage facilities across the US; occupancy and the ability to raise rents on existing tenants matter more than new development.
OXY: Produces oil and gas in the Permian and Middle East, owns a chemicals business, and is building direct air capture plants — the last funded partly by policy credits.
CVE: Canadian integrated producer: oil sands production feeding refineries it part-owns in the US Midwest, which hedges the heavy crude differential.
LITE: Makes the optical components and lasers that carry traffic between AI accelerators and between data centres; demand now tracks cloud capital spending rather than telecom.
LNG: Owns and operates the Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi LNG export terminals, selling liquefaction capacity on twenty-year take-or-pay contracts rather than selling gas.
FAST: Distributes fasteners and industrial supplies through branches and vending machines placed inside customers' own plants, which is what makes the relationship hard to displace.
KEYS: Sells the test and measurement instruments used to design and validate chips, wireless networks and cars; sold into engineering budgets rather than production ones.
CAH: Distributes prescription drugs to pharmacies and hospitals, and manufactures its own medical and surgical products — the third of the big three US drug distributors.
ROK: Sells factory automation — programmable controllers, drives, industrial software — to manufacturers, with the installed base and the engineers trained on it the switching cost.
